summary: Describes an anycasting service for IP, in which a packet goes to any one of a group of hosts that provide the same service. It mainly establishes what such a service should mean.

eli5.summary: If you shout for help and the closest of many helpers comes, you did anycast. This memo explains how that could work for Internet packets.

questions: how does anycast work with tcp
what are the security issues with anycast
subtitle: The original definition of IP anycast: send a packet to an address and let the network deliver it to the nearest of many servers.

tldr.problem: A host often wants any one server that offers a service and does not care which, but has to choose from a list of servers and guess which is closest.
tldr.mechanism: An anycast address stands for a group of servers. The network makes a best-effort, stateless delivery of each datagram to at least one, and preferably only one, of them.
tldr.outcome: The memo establishes the semantics and discusses address, link-level, UDP and TCP issues. It describes an experimental service and does not propose a protocol.

facts.label: TCP rule
facts.value: Anycast only as remote address of a SYN without ACK

today: RFC 1546 is an Informational memo from November 1993, produced by the IRTF, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an experimental service and proposes no protocol, so it is best read as the statement of what IP anycast should mean.

sections.title: Why Anycasting
sections.content:
Sometimes a host, application or user wants a server for a service and does not care which one it gets. With anycasting, a host sends a datagram to an anycast address, and the internetwork provides best-effort delivery to at least one, and preferably only one, of the servers that accept datagrams for that address.

The RFC offers three examples: typing telnet archie.net and reaching the nearest archie server, DNS resolvers sending queries to a well-known DNS anycast address instead of being configured with server addresses, and mirrored FTP sites sharing a single anycast address.

This memo is produced by the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF). It describes an experimental service and does not propose a protocol.
sections.eli5: Instead of picking from a long list of helpers, you ask for any helper and the closest one answers.

sections.title: What Anycast Means, and Its Addresses
sections.content:
The hard question is how to square IP's stateless service with an address that stands for a single virtual host. If two servers X and Y share an anycast address, can one datagram reach both? Yes: IP is allowed to duplicate and misroute datagrams, so delivery to both is permissible. Can two datagrams from the same sender go to different servers? Also yes, because IP cannot track where earlier datagrams went.

So the RFC defines IP anycasting as a stateless best-effort delivery of an anycast datagram to at least one host, and preferably only one, that serves the address. Anycast datagrams get the same basic type of service as other IP datagrams.

Anything that needs a series of datagrams to reach the same peer has to add its own mechanism, because the network gives no such guarantee.

The memo weighs three ways to provide anycast addresses. Carving them from existing site address space may make routing easier, but TCP has no easy way to tell an address is anycast and well-known Internet-wide anycast addresses are harder. A separate class of addresses makes anycast easy to recognize and well-known addresses easier, but routing protocols may have to track more routes. An intermediate approach uses part of the current space, such as 256 Class C addresses, but wastes address space.

On balance the RFC assumes anycast addresses will be a separate class of IP addresses, not yet assigned. Because the number of anycasting hosts seems unlikely to exceed the number of services offered by protocols like TCP and UDP, the space could be small, perhaps as little as 2**16 addresses.
sections.eli5:
The network promises to try to reach one helper, but not the same helper every time, so you can not count on talking to the same one twice.

Anycast addresses should get their own special range, like a separate set of phone numbers just for hotlines, so everyone can tell them apart.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Anycast Datagrams
sections.content:
Hosts are not required to take part in routing, and IP is meant to work without routers on a LAN. So on a shared medium such as Ethernet or Token Ring, it must be possible to reach a local anycast server without a router. The RFC describes two ways. A host can ARP for the anycast address and send to the first server that replies, which needs ARP cache timeouts kept small (around 1 minute). Or it can send on a link-level multicast address that anycast servers listen to, at the cost that every local server receives the message.

On point-to-point links, one copy is forwarded along the link toward the destination. Routers forward one copy toward the next hop, and should avoid forwarding a datagram if another router will also be forwarding it.

Servers must advertise that they have joined an anycast address. On shared media this is probably best done by periodically multicasting the information, possibly using an enhanced IGMP; on point-to-point links the host tells the router at the other end. A host that receives a datagram for an anycast address it supports handles it like any other datagram, and silently discards it if it does not support the address. Hosts should accept datagrams with an anycast source address, although some transport protocols may refuse them.
sections.eli5: Nearby computers can shout on the local network and take the first answer, while helpers tell their routers which special addresses they answer to.

sections.title: UDP, TCP and Applications
sections.content:
UDP is stateless like anycast, so it can treat an anycast address like any other address. TCP is stateful, so the RFC allows an anycast address only as the remote address of a TCP SYN segment without the ACK bit set. When the SYN-ACK comes back, the initiating TCP replaces the anycast address of its peer with the address of the host that sent the SYN-ACK. From then on it talks to exactly one host.

Applications that keep state over UDP, or across several TCP connections, cannot assume the same peer answers twice. The suggested fix is to learn the peer's unicast address on the first exchange and use it afterwards.
sections.eli5: For a phone call you need the same person the whole time, so after the first answer you switch to that person's own number.

sections.title: Anycast Compared with Multicast
sections.content:
An anycast address is the address of a single virtual host, so senders need not manage TTLs and a TCP connection to one makes sense. Finding a server by multicast means sending and resending with successively larger IP TTLs, so more datagrams are sent and some expire before reaching a server. Anycast is a special use of unicast addressing, and multiple routes to an anycast address look like multiple routes to a unicast destination, so routers can use standard algorithms to choose the best.

Anycast may be less fault tolerant: when a server fails, some datagrams may still be routed to it, while a multicast datagram would also reach other servers.
sections.eli5: Multicast is shouting louder and louder until someone answers. Anycast is asking the network to hand your message to one nearby helper.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC mentions two security issues and offers no solutions. Malevolent hosts could volunteer to serve an anycast address and divert datagrams from legitimate servers. Eavesdropping hosts could reply to anycast queries with inaccurate information, and since there is no way to verify membership in an anycast address, such a reply can not be detected as coming from a non-member.
sections.eli5: A trickster could pretend to be a helper and answer in place of the real one, and the network has no way to check.
